---
title: "A picture made of text"
---

Last year you told p5.js what to draw, one command after another, and it
painted pixels onto a canvas. The browser can draw too, and it does it in a way
that looks strange for about five minutes: the picture is written as tags,
inside your HTML, where you can read it. Type one and see.

::: {.callout-note}
## New part, new buddy code

Part 3 has its own coding buddy, which knows SVG the way the earlier one knew
the DOM. Your teacher hands out the code for it, and you put it into
`~/.pi/agent/auth.json` in place of the Part 2 code. The chapter on your coding
buddy shows that file.
:::

## A circle you can read {#sec-svg-by-hand-circle}

1. Create a new app `svg-experiment` from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace the `<h1>` line with this:

   ```html
   <svg viewBox="0 0 200 200" width="200" role="img" aria-label="A gold circle">
     <circle cx="100" cy="100" r="60" fill="gold" stroke="black" stroke-width="4" />
   </svg>
   ```

3. Delete both lines in `src/index.ts`. They talked to the heading you just
   replaced, so leave the file empty for the moment.
4. Look at the browser.

A gold circle with a black outline, 200 pixels wide. Change `r="60"` to
`r="90"` and save. Change the fill to `fill="tomato"` and save. Each time, the
browser has the new picture on screen before your hand is off the keyboard.

The pair `role="img" aria-label="A gold circle"` is the picture's alternative
text, and a screen reader announces it instead of reading out shapes it cannot
describe. Biome's accessibility rule refuses an `<svg>` without such a name, so
put the pair on every drawing you write.

Now press F12 and open the **Elements** tab. There is your `<circle>`, a line
in the tree next to your headings and buttons. Double click the `60` in
`r="60"`, type `20`, and press Enter: the circle shrinks. A shape is an element,
with a tag name and attributes, living in the DOM exactly like a `<p>` does.

## The same rings, twice {#sec-svg-by-hand-rings}

Year one ended its first part with the Olympic rings. Five circles, no fill,
a fat outline, three on top and two hanging below:

```ts
function setup() {
  createCanvas(400, 200);
  noFill();
  strokeWeight(5);
  stroke('blue');
  circle(100, 100, 80);
  stroke('black');
  circle(200, 100, 80);
  stroke('red');
  circle(300, 100, 80);
  // yellow at (150, 140) and green at (250, 140) take the same two lines each
}
```

Here are the same five rings as SVG. Put them into your `index.html` in place of
the gold circle and compare them with the picture you drew last year:

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 200" width="400" role="img" aria-label="The five Olympic rings">
  <circle cx="100" cy="100" r="40" fill="none" stroke="blue" stroke-width="5" />
  <circle cx="200" cy="100" r="40" fill="none" stroke="black" stroke-width="5" />
  <circle cx="300" cy="100" r="40" fill="none" stroke="red" stroke-width="5" />
  <circle cx="150" cy="140" r="40" fill="none" stroke="yellow" stroke-width="5" />
  <circle cx="250" cy="140" r="40" fill="none" stroke="green" stroke-width="5" />
</svg>
```

Same rings, two ways of thinking. The p5.js version is a list of orders in a
fixed sequence: switch the fill off, set the thickness, set a color, draw a
circle, set the next color, draw the next one. The settings stay in force until
a later line changes them, so moving a single `stroke` line repaints half the
picture in the wrong color.

The SVG version orders nobody around. It says what is there: five circles, each
with its own place, size, and color, each carrying everything it needs. Reading
it out loud describes the finished picture, not the way there.

Programmers call the first style **imperative**, from a word for command: you
write the steps and the machine follows them. The second is **declarative**:
you write what the result should be and let the machine work out the steps.
The difference pays off when the picture has to change. In p5.js you clear the
canvas and run all the drawing commands again. In SVG you change the one
attribute you mean, and the browser redraws that shape by itself.

## The drawing brings its own coordinates {#sec-svg-by-hand-viewbox}

`viewBox="0 0 400 200"` sets up the coordinate system inside the drawing. The
four numbers are the x and y where the drawing starts, then its width and its
height. Every `cx`, `cy`, `x`, and `r` inside is counted in those units, never
in pixels.

`width="400"` is a different measurement: it says how much room the drawing
takes on the page. Write `width="200"` instead and the whole picture shrinks to
half size, outlines and all, without touching a single coordinate. That is the
scalable in Scalable Vector Graphics.

The y axis points down, the way it did on the p5.js canvas: 0,0 is the top left
corner, and a bigger y moves a shape further down.

## Shapes are elements, one tag each {#sec-svg-by-hand-shapes}

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 120" width="200" role="img" aria-label="One shape of each kind">
  <rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="40" rx="8" fill="lightblue" />
  <line x1="10" y1="70" x2="90" y2="70" stroke="black" stroke-width="3" />
  <polygon points="120,10 190,10 155,50" fill="seagreen" />
  <path d="M 120 100 L 190 100 L 155 60 Z" fill="none" stroke="purple" stroke-width="3" />
  <text x="10" y="110" font-size="14">Hello SVG</text>
</svg>
```

A `rect` is placed by its top left corner, and `rx` rounds the corners off. A
`line` gets the two ends it runs between, and it needs a `stroke`: a line has no
inside, so a fill has nothing to color and the line stays invisible. A `polygon`
takes a list of `points` and closes the shape for you.

`path` is the shape that can draw anything, and its `d` attribute is a little
language of its own. `M 120 100` moves the pen to a point without drawing,
`L 190 100` draws a straight line to the next point, and `Z` closes the shape
back to where the `M` started. Those three letters already give you every
triangle and every zigzag.

`text` puts letters on the drawing. Its `y` is the baseline, the line the
letters sit on, so `y="110"` means the bottom of the letters is at 110, not the
top.

Two attributes decide how a shape looks: `fill` colors the inside, `stroke`
colors the outline, and `stroke-width` says how thick that outline is. A shape
with no `fill` attribute is filled black, and one with no `stroke` has no
outline at all.

Shapes that belong together go into a `g`, a group. Attributes on the group
count for everything inside it, which saves repeating the same `fill` on eight
dots:

```html
<g fill="black">
  <circle cx="40" cy="40" r="7" />
  <circle cx="90" cy="40" r="7" />
</g>
```

There are more shapes than these, and far more attributes.
[MDN's SVG element reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Element)
lists every one of them with an example. Keep that page open while you draw.

## A picture in its own file {#sec-svg-by-hand-file}

An SVG drawing does not need a page around it. Create a file `rings.svg` in the
`assets/` folder of your project, and put the rings in it with one extra
attribute on the `<svg>` tag:

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" width="400" role="img" aria-label="The five Olympic rings">
  <circle cx="100" cy="100" r="40" fill="none" stroke="blue" stroke-width="5" />
  <!-- the other four circles, exactly as in your page -->
</svg>
```

Inside an HTML page, the `<svg>` tag itself tells the browser that the tags
inside it are shapes. A file on its own gets no such hint, and `circle` could
mean anything. The attribute `xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"` names the
vocabulary the tags come from. Leave it out of a stand-alone file and the
browser shows you text or an error instead of a picture.

Open `http://localhost:5173/assets/rings.svg` in a browser tab and the rings
appear on their own, with no HTML anywhere. The same file opens in a drawing
program such as Inkscape, because SVG is a standard that everybody reads.

To get the file onto your page, use it like any other image:

```html
<img src="/assets/rings.svg" alt="The five Olympic rings" width="400">
```

Now try to color the shapes from CSS. Put this into `src/styles.css` and import
the stylesheet from `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';`:

```css
circle:hover {
  fill: tomato;
}
```

Hover the outline of a ring you wrote into `index.html`, the thin line itself,
and the ring fills with red. Hover the rings inside the `<img>` and nothing
happens. To the page that `<img>` is one picture, and its shapes sit in another
file, outside this page's DOM. Written inline, every shape is in the DOM, so CSS
selectors reach it and from the next chapter on your TypeScript does too. That
is why the rest of this part writes SVG inline.

::: {.research title="Curves, line ends, and centered text"}
The smiley in the exercise below needs a curved mouth, and the `L` command only
draws straight lines. The domino next to it needs a label that stays centered
under the tile.

1. The `A` command of a `path` takes seven numbers, as in
   `A 55 45 0 0 0 145 115`. What does each number mean? Name at least the two
   radii, the large-arc flag, the sweep flag, and the end point.
2. What does `stroke-linecap="round"` change about a `<line>`, and what do the
   line's ends look like without it?
3. What does `text-anchor="middle"` do to a `<text>` element, measured against
   its `x`?

The two flags of `A` and `text-anchor` are exam material: the exam has no
internet and no AI next to you.
:::

## Exercise: smiley and domino {#sec-svg-by-hand-exercise}

Year one's smiley comes back, this time written as tags, and a domino tile
stands next to it. Everything is hand-written SVG in `index.html`, so there is
no TypeScript in this exercise beyond one import.

1. Create a new app `smiley-domino` from our template inside `homework/`.
2. Replace both lines in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';`, and
   create an empty `src/styles.css` next to it.
3. In `index.html`, replace the `<h1>` line with an `<svg>` that has
   `viewBox="0 0 200 200"`, `width="200"`, `role="img"`, an `aria-label` of
   `A smiley face`, and one `circle` for the face: `cx="100"`, `cy="100"`,
   `r="90"`, `fill="gold"`, `stroke="black"`, `stroke-width="5"`. Keep the
   `<script>` line at the end of the body. Expected result: a big gold face.
4. Add the eyes: two circles with `r="8"` and `fill="black"`, both at
   `cy="75"`, one at `cx="70"` and one at `cx="130"`. Give both of them
   `class="eye"`.
5. Add the mouth as a `path` with `fill="none"`, `stroke="black"`, and
   `stroke-width="5"`. Its `d` starts at `M 55 115` and then uses one `A`
   command with the radii 55 and 45 to reach the end point `145 115`. Choose
   the three numbers in between so the mouth smiles, which means it bulges
   downward. Expected result: a friendly face. Flip the sweep flag once, save,
   and watch the smiley turn sad.
6. Below the first drawing, start a second `<svg>` for the domino, with
   `viewBox="0 0 120 230"`, `width="120"`, and an `aria-label` of its own next
   to `role="img"`. Draw the tile as a `rect` at `x="10"`, `y="10"`, with
   `width="100"`, `height="190"`, `rx="12"`, `fill="white"`, `stroke="black"`,
   and `stroke-width="4"`. Expected result: an upright tile with rounded
   corners.
7. Divide the tile with a `line` from `10,105` to `110,105`, in black and
   `stroke-width="4"`.
8. Put the dots in. Every dot is a circle with `r="7"`, and all of them go into
   one `g` with `fill="black"` so no dot repeats the color. The top half shows
   3: three dots on a diagonal running from the upper left to the lower right.
   The bottom half shows 5: one dot in each corner of that half and one in the
   middle. Work out the coordinates yourself, and keep every dot at least 10
   units away from the border and from the dividing line.
9. Label the tile with a `text` element under it, at `x="60"` and `y="222"`,
   with `font-size="16"` and `text-anchor="middle"`, reading `3 : 5`. Expected
   result: the label sits centered below the tile. Delete the `text-anchor`
   attribute once and watch the label slide to the right.
10. In `src/styles.css`, make the eyes react to the mouse: a rule for `.eye`
    with `:hover` that sets `fill` to `royalblue`. Expected result: pointing at
    an eye turns it blue, and the rest of the face stays as it is.
11. Optional: put the two drawings side by side. `body { display: flex; gap:
    2rem; align-items: flex-start; }` in your stylesheet is enough.
12. Run `npm run check`. If Biome complains that an alternative text title
    element cannot be empty, one of your two drawings is missing its
    `role="img"` and `aria-label`.
